security_audit.summary: Seven findings confirm intended local CLI execution, including installation, authentication, diagnostics, and factor queries. Most remaining detections are Markdown syntax, official documentation links, or secure credential guidance. Two contextual risks remain: mutable global installation and weaker local credential storage.

remediation.issue: The installation command uses a mutable latest package version with global privileges.
remediation.suggestion: Pin a reviewed ccdb-cli version and provide an integrity check before global installation.

remediation.issue: The CLI may store encrypted credentials and their master key on the same machine.
remediation.suggestion: Require clear user confirmation before this fallback and recommend a system credential service whenever available.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 12 explicitly requires the host to execute ccdb-cli with network access and authorization. This is intended behavior, but it creates a real external-command trust boundary.
Line 14 directs execution of a version check and conditionally proceeds to installation. User consent limits the risk but does not remove external command execution.
Lines 16 through 18 contain a shell block that globally installs ccdb-cli from npm and then executes it. The mutable package and global scope create supply-chain and host-modification risk.
Line 19 is only the closing marker for a Markdown shell block. It performs no Ruby or shell backtick execution.
The backticks on line 27 format profile names and environment settings as inline Markdown. They are not executable shell substitution.
Line 29 directs the host to run ccdb-cli authentication commands after user consent. This invokes an external program and opens an OAuth authorization flow.
Line 31 directs execution of ccdb-cli API-key authentication using controlled input. The handling guidance is careful, but the command crosses a credential-bearing process boundary.
Line 34 explicitly directs execution of ccdb-cli status and diagnostic commands. These commands can inspect local authentication state and discovered endpoints.
Lines 40 through 42 contain shell commands that search CCDB and retrieve factor details. This is the intended feature but requires external process and network execution.
Line 43 is a closing Markdown fence. The following text describes ID and profile consistency without shell backtick substitution.
Line 47 uses backticks only to format supported CLI options. It does not execute those values or construct a command.
Line 57 formats the response field name detailUrl with Markdown backticks. No external command is present.
Line 59 formats API response field names with Markdown backticks. These references are data-handling guidance, not shell execution.
Line 65 uses inline code formatting for factorId and masked or missing values. It explicitly prevents unsafe guessing and contains no command.
Line 66 formats a guidance code and response field names. It contains no external process invocation.
Line 67 formats verified=false as response metadata. The text preserves provenance and does not execute a command.
Line 70 formats an OAuth error name. The surrounding recovery guidance discourages guessing identifiers and replaying tokens.
Line 71 formats a credential-store error code and links to documentation. It does not contain shell backtick execution.
Line 21 links to the official carbonstop ccdb-cli GitHub release and repository pages. The URLs support manual installation and documentation without transmitting user data.
Line 27 links to the official carbonstop ccdb-cli configuration document. It also prohibits automatic environment switching or configuration rewriting.
Line 71 links to the official carbonstop ccdb-cli repository for troubleshooting. No credentials or collected data are appended to the URL.
Line 31 names CCDB_API_KEY while requiring secure host configuration or non-echoing input. Lines 31 and 32 prohibit providing the key in chat or command arguments.
SKILL.md is readable Chinese Markdown with YAML metadata and ordinary documentation. No binary, encrypted, encoded, or intentionally obscured payload is present.

content.user_title: Find and Compare CCDB Emission Factors
content.value_statement: Choosing an emission factor requires careful checks across units, geography, time, technology, source, and accounting boundaries. This skill searches CCDB and explains candidate suitability.
actual_capabilities: Searches CCDB emission factors through ccdb-cli with a result limit.
Retrieves factor details using an identifier returned by the current search.
Filters by language, accounting type, country, year, and source level.
Compares units, geography, time, technology, boundaries, and data sources.
Preserves factor values, identifiers, verification status, and source limitations.
Provides returned CCDB detail links when they are safe and available.
limitations: Requires ccdb-cli, network access, and valid CCDB authorization.
Does not write models or replace a complete carbon assessment or compliance review.
Cannot use masked, missing, or restricted values for calculations.
Does not invent conversion parameters, factor identifiers, values, or links.

use_cases.title: Select a Product Footprint Factor
use_cases.description: Compare material factors against a product boundary, production route, geography, year, and required unit.

use_cases.title: Match Corporate Activity Data
use_cases.description: Find electricity, fuel, transport, or purchased-material factors that match an organizational inventory.

use_cases.title: Review LCA Dataset Candidates
use_cases.description: Inspect source, system boundary, technology, location, and temporal fit before selecting a dataset.

prompt_templates.title: Basic Factor Search
prompt_templates.prompt: Search CCDB for electricity emission factors in Germany and show up to five relevant results.
prompt_templates.scenario: Start with a material or activity and a known location.

prompt_templates.title: Filter by Accounting Context
prompt_templates.prompt: Find 2024 natural gas factors for a corporate inventory in France, then explain each result's unit and source.
prompt_templates.scenario: Apply time, location, and accounting filters.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Material Candidates
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare CCDB factors for recycled aluminum sheet in China by boundary, production route, unit, year, and source.
prompt_templates.scenario: Evaluate several candidates for a product footprint.

prompt_templates.title: Assess Advanced Factor Fit
prompt_templates.prompt: Match this activity dataset to CCDB factors, identify missing selection criteria, inspect details, and document assumptions and mismatches: [describe dataset].
prompt_templates.scenario: Perform a structured suitability review with incomplete requirements.

output_examples.input: Find electricity factors for a 2023 corporate inventory in Germany.
output: Candidate: linked CCDB factor name and identifier.
Fit: Germany, corporate accounting, and the stated applicable year.
Review: confirm unit, electricity scope, source, and system boundary before calculation.

output_examples.input: Compare recycled and primary aluminum factors for a product footprint.
output: Primary aluminum: source, geography, year, unit, route, and boundary summary.
Recycled aluminum: source, geography, year, unit, route, and boundary summary.
Recommendation: select only after confirming product form and recycling process.

output_examples.output: The factor value is restricted in this response. Review the returned Carbon Agent link for its source and applicable scope.

best_practices: Specify the activity, accounting context, unit, geography, year, technology, and boundary before selecting a factor.
Open factor details before recommending a specific result.
Preserve returned values and limitations, and distinguish CCDB data from user values or external estimates.
anti_patterns: Do not treat every search result as a final recommendation.
Do not convert masked or missing values to zero or infer restricted data.
Do not switch environments, identities, credentials, or legacy endpoints to bypass access limits.

faq.question: What does this skill search?
faq.answer: It searches Carbonstop CCDB for emission factors covering materials, energy, transport, packaging, food, and other activities.

faq.question: What access is required?
faq.answer: The host needs ccdb-cli, local command execution, network access, and valid CCDB authorization.

faq.question: Can it select a factor automatically?
faq.answer: It compares suitability and explains tradeoffs, but the user must confirm the accounting context and assumptions.

faq.question: Does it support product and corporate accounting?
faq.answer: Yes. It can filter for product or enterprise accounting, but factors from those contexts are not directly interchangeable.

faq.question: How are restricted values handled?
faq.answer: The skill reports the restriction and provides a returned review link when available. It does not guess the hidden value.

faq.question: Does it perform a complete carbon calculation?
faq.answer: No. It finds and assesses factors, but it does not replace full modeling, calculation, verification, or compliance review.
